Short case 22 · General Surgery

Lymphoedema

A swollen limb whose dorsal skin you cannot pinch. That one sign, Stemmer's, separates lymphoedema from every other cause of a swollen leg, and it is the case in a sentence. Then two questions: is it primary or secondary, and has the skin changed yet, because the skin decides the treatment.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework
Read this before you look for lymphoedema in Bailey & Love The 28th edition has no lymphatic system chapter. There are exactly three places where lymphoedema appears, and none of them is a chapter on the subject:

1. Chapter 6, "Tropical infections and infestations", pp.72 and 73, under FILARIASIS. This is the only substantive discussion, and it is about filarial lymphoedema and elephantiasis specifically.​B&L 6 · p.72​B&L 6 · p.73
2. Chapter 45, p.661, one sentence under angiosarcoma: the lymphangiosarcoma variant "arises from lymphatic endothelium and can develop in lymphoedematous tissue, particularly an extremity".​B&L 45 · p.661
3. Chapter 58, breast, as a complication of axillary treatment: "the axilla should not be irradiated after axillary node dissection as this increases the risk of lymphoedema."​B&L 58 · p.939

So everything else in this case is S Das ch.8 and SRB ch.1. Do not waste time looking for Kinmonth's classification, Browse's classification, Milroy's disease, lymphoedema praecox, the grading, lymphoscintigraphy or the named operations in Bailey & Love 28e. None of them is there. Knowing that is itself useful: it tells you which book to quote at the bedside.

1Definition and mechanism

Definition
SRB: "It is accumulation of fluid (lymph) in extracellular and extravascular fluid compartment, commonly in subcutaneous tissue. It is primarily due to defective lymphatic drainage. It is increased protein rich interstitial fluid."​SRB 1 · p.241 S Das: "lymphoedema is caused by accumulation of lymph within the tissues. It mainly affects the subcutaneous tissues of the limbs. This is due to stagnation of lymph within the lymphatics."​Das 8 · p.114
The three words that matterProtein rich. That is what distinguishes it from every other oedema and explains the whole natural history: protein in the interstitium drives fibrosis, fibrosis makes the oedema non-pitting, and non-pitting oedema does not respond to elevation.
The pathophysiological sequence, which is the best answer to "why does the skin change?"
SRB sets it out as a chain, and it is worth reciting in order: decreased lymphatic contractility, valvular insufficiency, or obliteration by infection, tumour or surgery leads to "lymphatic hypertension and dilatation causing lymph stasis, accumulation of proteins, glycosamines, growth factors, and bacteria. There is more collagen formation, deposition of proteins, fibroblasts, ground substance causing fibrosis in subcutaneous and outside deep fascia."​SRB 1 · p.242 Then: "activation of collagens and keratinocytes", "dermal thickening and dermal proliferation", cracks, ulceration, abscess, and finally elephantiasis.​SRB 1 · p.244
The detail examiners like"Muscles are normal without any oedema but may get hypertrophied."​SRB 1 · p.242 The disease is outside the deep fascia. That is why the limb is heavy but not weak, and why one class of operation works by cutting windows in the deep fascia.
The anatomical fact the operations are built on
SRB states it explicitly, and it is the single best thing to know about this condition: "disease in the limb is confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue, i.e. often, only superficial lymphatics are involved by the disease, deep lymphatics are not. Superficial and deep lymphatics are not communicating with each other (unlike the veins in the limb where superficial and deep veins are freely communicating with each other)."​SRB 1 · p.244
Why this is the key to the vivaBecause it explains, in one stroke, why the leg swells although the deep system is healthy, and why every "physiological" operation ever devised has the same aim: to create a communication between the diseased superficial lymphatics and the healthy deep ones. Sistrunk's windows in the deep fascia, Thompson's buried dermal flap, the nodovenous and lymphovenous shunts, the ileal mucosal patch, omentoplasty: all of them are attempts to build that missing connection.

2Classification: both systems, and when to use each

Kinmonth's, which is the one to open with
Primary, "without any identifiable lymphatic disease"; and secondary, "acquired due to definitive cause. Most common form."​SRB 1 · p.242 Note that last phrase, because candidates assume primary is commoner.
Primary, subdivided by age of onset: the three names
Lymphoedema congenita, present at birth to under 2 years, 10%. The familial form is Nonne-Milroy's disease: "type I familial, autosomal dominant, chromosome 5 related; bilateral upper and lower limbs, genitalia and face may be involved. Incidence is 1 in 6000 of live births."​SRB 1 · p.242
Lymphoedema praecox, at puberty up to about 35 years, 80%, so much the commonest primary form. The familial form is Letessier-Meige's syndrome, type II familial.​SRB 1 · p.242
Lymphoedema tarda, in adult life after 35 years.​SRB 1 · p.242
And the syndromes to namePrimary lymphoedema can be syndromic: Turner's, Klinefelter's, Down's, Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber. It "affects commonly females" and is "common in lower limb and left side".​SRB 1 · p.242
Browse's lymphangiographic classification, which an examiner may ask for by name
Classifies by what the lymphangiogram shows rather than by when the swelling started, which makes it the more useful of the two for planning treatment:​SRB 1 · p.241
Congenital hyperplasia, 10%. "Common in males; entire leg is involved; one or both sides; with often family history; progressive; involves increased number of lymphatics and lymph nodes associated with chylous ascites, chylothorax and protein losing enteropathy."
Distal obliteration, 80%. "Common in females; starts at puberty; calf and ankle are involved; often bilateral; with often family history; slow progression; aplasia/hypoplasia of lymphatics."
Proximal obliteration, 10%. "Occurs at any age; equal in both sexes; leg and thigh involved; unilateral; rapid progression; proximal aortoiliac nodal block."
How to tell them apart at the bedside, which is what Browse is for Distal disease is bilateral, slowly progressive, starts at the ankle and affects young women. Proximal disease is unilateral, rapidly progressive and involves the thigh, and because the block is at the aortoiliac nodes it is the one in which you must look hard for a pelvic malignancy. That distinction changes what you do next, which is why it earns marks. A caution about the percentagesSRB's own radiological breakdown on the next page gives hypoplasia 70%, aplasia 15%, hyperplasia 15%, which does not quite reconcile with Browse's 10 / 80 / 10.​SRB 1 · p.242 Quote one set or the other, not both in the same breath.
Secondary: the causes, with the commonest first
SRB's list, and the order to give it in depends on where you are:​SRB 1 · p.242
Surgery, specifically "inguinal block or axillary block dissection, post-mastectomy with axillary clearance". S Das's illustration is exactly this: lymphoedema of the arm following radical mastectomy,​Das 8 · p.114 and he notes secondary lymphoedema "often follows operation like extirpation of lymph nodes, e.g. radical mastectomy".​Das 8 · p.114
Filarial, "due to Wuchereria bancrofti, common cause in coastal region". S Das: "lymphoedema following filariasis is more common in tropical countries and Orissa seems to be the most affected state in India."​Das 8 · p.114
Advanced malignancy, "hard, fixed lymph nodes in axilla or in inguinal region".
Post-radiotherapy. B&L's version of this is the practical rule: "the axilla should not be irradiated after axillary node dissection as this increases the risk of lymphoedema."​B&L 58 · p.939 Surgery plus radiotherapy to the same basin is the combination that causes it.
Infection: tuberculosis, syphilis, fungal and bacterial.
Trauma, and rarely rheumatoid arthritis, snake and insect bites, deep vein thrombosis and chronic venous insufficiency.
And the timing clueSRB: "secondary lymphoedema develops rapidly."​SRB 1 · p.242 S Das makes the same contrast: primary lymphoedema is "slowly progressive swelling of the limb and the genitalia which takes even years to develop", whereas secondary "is often associated with some sort of complaints" that point to the cause.​Das 8 · p.114
One cause neither of the other books gives, worth a sentence
Podoconiosis. SRB: "endemic elephantiasis or podoconiosis is common in Africa; seen in barefoot workers; due to destruction of lymphatics by silica derived from soil containing alkaline volcanic rocks."​SRB 1 · p.244 Non-infective, non-filarial elephantiasis from walking barefoot on volcanic soil. If you can name it, do.

3History

1. How old was the patient when it started? It is the axis of the whole primary classification. S Das: "primary lymphoedema may reveal itself in young age, whereas secondary lymphoedema mostly presents in middle and old ages."​Das 8 · p.114 Onset at birth means congenita, at puberty praecox, after 35 tarda.​SRB 1 · p.242 Say the name, then the age bracket"Onset at puberty puts this in lymphoedema praecox, which is 80% of primary lymphoedema." That is worth more than describing the swelling.
2. Male or female, and is there a family history? S Das: "somehow or other females are more affected than males so far as primary lymphoedema is concerned. Even secondary lymphoedema is more common in women following radical mastectomy or due to involvement of the iliac and inguinal nodes from malignant tumours of the uterus or ovary."​Das 8 · p.114 A family history points to Nonne-Milroy's (autosomal dominant) or Letessier-Meige's.​SRB 1 · p.242 And the one exceptionB&L's filarial disease runs the other way: "it is mainly males who are affected because females generally cover a greater part of their bodies with clothing, thus making them less prone to mosquito bites."​B&L 6 · p.72 So a filarial leg in an endemic area is more often a man's; a primary lymphoedema is more often a woman's.
3. Where does he live, or where has he lived? Because filariasis is geographical and it is the commonest cause in much of India. B&L: filariasis "affects more than 120 million people worldwide, two-thirds of whom live in India, China and Indonesia. According to the World Health Organization, after leprosy, filariasis is the most common cause of long-term disability."​B&L 6 · p.72 SRB adds that filarial lymphoedema is the "common cause in coastal region",​SRB 1 · p.242 and S Das names Orissa as the most affected Indian state.​Das 8 · p.114
4. Has there been an operation, radiotherapy or a cancer? Because secondary lymphoedema is the commonest form overall, and the cause is almost always in the history rather than on examination. Ask about mastectomy with axillary clearance, inguinal or ilioinguinal block dissection, radiotherapy to the axilla or groin, and any known malignancy.​SRB 1 · p.242 The example SRB illustratesLymphoedema of the lower limb developed after ilioinguinal block dissection for nodal secondaries from melanoma.​SRB 1 · p.244
5. Has he had repeated attacks of fever with a red, painful limb? Because recurrent lymphangitis is both a symptom of lymphoedema and the engine that worsens it, and that circularity is the point. B&L: "in the acute presentation, there are episodic attacks of fever with lymphadenitis and lymphangitis", and later "recurrent attacks of lymphangitis cause fibrosis of the lymph channels, resulting in a grossly swollen limb with thickened skin, producing the condition of elephantiasis."​B&L 6 · p.72 SRB lists minor trauma and lymphoedema as the precipitating factors for acute lymphangitis, and "development of lymphoedema" as one of its complications.​SRB 1 · p.241 So say the vicious circle out loudLymph stasis invites infection; infection scars the remaining lymphatics; more scarring means more stasis. That is why antibiotics, skin care and antifungals are not minor adjuncts in this disease but the main long-term treatment. B&L notes "secondary streptococcal infection is common".​B&L 6 · p.72
6. Is there pain, and how disabling is it? Candidates assume lymphoedema is painless. SRB: "dull ache, severe pain, burning, bursting, cramps; 50% patients will have pain."​SRB 1 · p.244 It also lists "debility, immobility, obesity, muscle wasting" and "psychological and social discomfort causing severe morbidity".​SRB 1 · p.244 S Das, by contrast, says "not many complaints are associated with this disease particularly the primary lymphoedema".​Das 8 · p.114 What to sayHalf have pain, and the disability is what the patient actually comes about. B&L's judgement on the advanced disease is blunt: "gross forms of the disease cause a great deal of disability and misery."​B&L 6 · p.73
7. Any milky urine, milky ascites or a swollen scrotum? Because these are the manifestations that confirm lymphatic obstruction elsewhere. B&L: "chyluria and chylous ascites may occur", and "bilateral lower limb filariasis is often associated with scrotal and penile elephantiasis. Early on, there may be a hydrocele underlying scrotal filariasis."​B&L 6 · pp.72, 73 SRB adds "protein losing diarrhoea, chylous ascites, chylothorax, chyluria, lymphorrhoea".​SRB 1 · p.244 And one respiratory form to nameTropical pulmonary eosinophilia: B&L, "a mild form of the disease can affect the respiratory tract, causing dry cough".​B&L 6 · p.73

4Examination: the signs, and Stemmer's first

Before you touch the patient The examiner is marking this before you have found anything. Bailey & Love gives it as a sequence: "ensure you have followed appropriate hand hygiene guidance. Introduce yourself and check the patient's name and date of birth. Request presence of a chaperone as appropriate. Explain what you are going to do, obtain verbal consent and ensure that the patient is comfortable."​B&L 35 · p.472 And the standard it is held to: "patients should be treated with respect and dignity, receive a clear explanation of the examination undertaken and be kept as comfortable as possible. A chaperone should be present, especially for intimate examinations."​B&L 21 · p.285

Do it, and be heard doing itWash your hands. Introduce yourself. Say what you want to examine and why, and ask permission. Ask for a chaperone where the examination is intimate. Expose what you need and cover the rest. Warm your hands. Tell the patient what each step will feel like and that they can ask you to stop, examine the tender part last, and watch their face rather than only your hands. Cover them and thank them before you turn to the examiner.
Stemmer's sign, which is the one to lead with
SRB: "skin over the dorsum of foot cannot be pinched because of subcutaneous fibrosis, Stemmer's sign."​SRB 1 · p.244
Why it worksIn any other oedema the subcutaneous tissue is water-logged but loose, so you can pick up a fold of skin at the base of the second toe. In lymphoedema the protein-rich fluid has driven subdermal fibrosis, so skin and subcutis are welded together and will not lift. It is a test of fibrosis, not of fluid, which is why it is positive in lymphoedema and negative in cardiac, renal and hepatic oedema.
The shape of the limb, which is diagnostic at a glance
SRB's four descriptors, all worth learning as phrases:​SRB 1 · p.244
Tree trunk pattern leg: swelling in the foot extending progressively up the leg, with "loss of normal perimalleolar shape". The ankle becomes a column rather than a waist.
Buffalo hump on the dorsum of the foot.
Squaring of the toes.
Contrast with venous oedemaVenous oedema spares the toes and the dorsum of the foot and leaves the perimalleolar hollows; lymphoedema fills all three. If the toes are square and the ankle has no waist, it is lymphatic.
Pitting or non-pitting, and why you must say which
S Das: "in the early stage this oedema pits on pressure, but gradually the subcutaneous tissue becomes fibrosed and the skin becomes keratotic (elephantiasis)."​Das 8 · p.114 SRB: "initially pitting oedema occurs, which later becomes non-pitting."​SRB 1 · p.244
This is not a detail, it is the treatment decisionPitting oedema is fluid, and fluid can be moved by elevation, compression and massage. Non-pitting oedema is fibrosis and deposited protein, and nothing short of excision will shift it. So the sentence "the oedema is non-pitting and the skin shows fibrosis and papillae" is what commits you to grade III and to a different answer on management.
The skin, in detail
Look for "eczema, fissuring, papillae formation, ulceration, lymph ooze, elephantiasis", and for athlete's foot, which SRB lists with "joint pain and disability".​SRB 1 · p.244 B&L explains why the skin thickens before the limb looks huge: "obstruction to the cutaneous lymphatics causes skin thickening, not unlike the peau d'orange appearance in breast cancer, thus exacerbating the limb swelling."​B&L 6 · p.72
And look between the toesInterdigital fungal infection is the commonest portal of entry for the streptococcus that causes the next attack of lymphangitis. Finding and treating it is an answer to "how would you prevent recurrence?"
What else to examine, and why each
Regional lymph nodes, for a cause: hard fixed nodes mean malignant obstruction. S Das: "in case of secondary lymphoedema examination must include regional lymph nodes and general examination to find out the diagnosis."​Das 8 · p.114
The scars of a previous mastectomy, axillary or groin dissection, or the skin changes of previous radiotherapy.
Abdomen and pelvis, in proximal-obliteration disease, for a mass blocking the aortoiliac nodes.
Subcutaneous nodules along the lymphatics. S Das: these occur "as in case of malignant melanoma and carcinoma. In case of malignant melanoma these nodules are often of deep brown to black colour."​Das 8 · p.114 And B&L adds the one finding unique to filariasis: "occasionally, adult worms may be felt subcutaneously."​B&L 6 · p.72
Acute lymphangitis, if present: "prominent lymphatic vessels as red streaks progressing towards the regional lymph nodes. There may be brawny oedema around."​Das 8 · p.114 SRB: "diffuse swelling in the skin with redness which blanches on pressure is typical", with fever, chills and tender regional nodes.​SRB 1 · p.241
And the sites other than the leg
Lower limb is commonest. Then upper limb; scrotum and penis (SRB's phrase for the penile form is "ram's horn penis"); breast, which "requires reduction mammoplasty"; labia; eyelid; and localised lymphoedema.​SRB 1 · p.244 S Das illustrates both lymphoedema of the arm after radical mastectomy and huge elephantiasis of both legs.​Das 8 · p.114
Grading, which is SRB's and SRB's alone, and which you will be asked Latent or subclinical: no clinically apparent lymphoedema.
Grade I: "pitting oedema which more or less disappears on elevation of the limb, is due to excess deposition of interstitial fluid."
Grade II: "non-pitting oedema occurs which does not reduce on elevation."
Grade III: "oedema with irreversible skin changes like fibrosis, papillae, fissuring."​SRB 1 · p.245

And a second, volumetric scale: mild, under 20% excess limb volume; moderate, 20 to 40%; severe, over 40%.​SRB 1 · p.245

Why the grade is the answer, not an ornament. Grade I is reversible by elevation, so conservative treatment is enough. Grade II has lost that reversibility, so it needs sustained compression. Grade III has fixed skin change, which is the only group in which excisional surgery is even discussed. Give the grade, then the treatment, and the treatment follows.

5Filariasis, because in India it is the cause you must know

The parasite and the vector
B&L: "filariasis is mainly caused by the parasite Wuchereria bancrofti, which is transmitted by the mosquito. Variants of the parasite called Brugia malayi and Brugia timori are responsible for causing the disease in about 10% of those infected."​B&L 6 · p.72 SRB names the Indian vector: Culex fatigans, with man the definitive host and the female mosquito the intermediate host; "animal or reservoir host is not known."​SRB 1 · p.242
Nocturnal periodicity, and the reason for it
SRB: "in India, Asian countries and China, they show nocturnal periodicity (from 10 PM to 4 AM). It is related to night biting habits of the vector, Culex fatigans mosquito and sleeping habits of the host."​SRB 1 · p.242
So the blood smear has a timeS Das puts it in his investigation list as "microfilaria in the peripheral blood vessels when the patient is sleeping".​Das 8 · p.115 B&L: "a nocturnal peripheral blood smear may show the immature forms, or microfilariae."​B&L 6 · p.73 Saying nocturnal and knowing why is a reliable mark.
The timings worth remembering
Maturation to adult worm takes almost a year after the bite, which is why the disease appears long after exposure.​B&L 6 · p.72 In the mosquito, "it takes 20 days for microfilaria to develop into infective 3rd stage larva".​SRB 1 · p.243 Life span of microfilaria in human blood is 3 months, and a gravid female releases up to 50 000 microfilariae a day into the lymph.​SRB 1 · p.243
And the fact that explains why the parasite load does not escalate SRB says it twice: "microfilaria never multiplies in mosquito nor in human", and "one microfilaria forms one infective larva".​SRB 1 · p.243 Disease severity comes from repeated bites over years, not from multiplication inside the host. That is why filarial elephantiasis is a disease of long residence in an endemic area.
Where the adult worms sit
B&L: "the adult worms mainly colonise the lymphatic system", and "the adult worms cause lymphatic obstruction, resulting in massive lower limb oedema."​B&L 6 · p.72 SRB is more specific: the infective larva "enters regional lymph nodes in inguinal or axillary or abdominal nodes" and develops into the adult worm in the lymph nodes.​SRB 1 · p.243
Where to find the parasite
B&L: "the parasite may also be seen in chylous urine, ascites and hydrocele fluid", and "eosinophilia is common".​B&L 6 · p.73 S Das lists eosinophilia under his blood examination as the finding "often seen in case of filariasis".​Das 8 · p.115

6Investigations

Blood
Eosinophilia for filariasis; nocturnal peripheral smear for microfilariae; raised ESR, which S Das associates with tuberculosis, secondary carcinoma and primary malignant lymphadenopathy.​Das 8 · p.115 SRB's minimum is "ESR, peripheral smear".​SRB 1 · p.246
For the cause, not the diagnosis
SRB: "for the cause, venous Doppler, US abdomen", and "MRI, CT scan to identify the cause".​SRB 1 · p.246
Why a venous Doppler in a lymphoedema caseTwo reasons, and both are good answers. To exclude deep venous disease, which is the main differential for a swollen limb; and because chronic venous insufficiency and deep vein thrombosis are themselves listed causes of secondary lymphoedema, so the two can coexist.​SRB 1 · p.242
Lymphangiography
S Das describes the technique: "injection of patent blue dye into the web between the toes will show lymphatics on the dorsum of the foot. One of these lymphatics is cannulated and ultrafluid lipiodol (radio-opaque dye) is injected to visualize on X-ray the main lymphatic channels of the leg and subsequently the lymph nodes."​Das 8 · p.116 SRB gives the rate: "injected slowly using pressure pump at a rate of 1 ml in 8 minutes (total quantity is 7 ml)", reaching iliac and para-aortic nodes over 24 hours.​SRB 1 · p.241
And the appearances S Das attaches to it"Irregular filling defect in the lymph node means secondary metastasis. Soap bubble or foamy appearance is seen in Hodgkin's disease. Coarse nodular storage pattern is seen in lymphosarcoma and marginal sunburst appearance is the feature found in reticulum cell sarcoma."​Das 8 · p.116
SRB's disadvantages, which is why it has been displaced "Technically difficult; extravasation of dye can occur; dye may not reach the required area; time consuming and invasive procedure."​SRB 1 · p.241
Isotope lymphoscintigraphy, and the numbers to quote
SRB: "radioactive technetium labelled sulphide colloid particles, or radioiodinated human albumin are injected into the web space using fine needle. These particles are specifically taken up by lymphatics." Radioactivity in the inguinal nodes is measured at 30 and 60 minutes: "normal uptake is 0.6–1.6%; if it is under 0.3% in 30 minutes it is diagnostic of lymphoedema. If it is over 2% it suggests rapid abnormal clearance due to oedema as the result of venous disease."​SRB 1 · p.241
SRB's verdict"It is the test of choice. It is simple and safe... it has 90% sensitivity; 100% specificity."​SRB 1 · p.241 It is more sensitive, technically easier and faster than lymphangiography, and it shows the thoracic duct, other nodes and the liver, and allows comparison with the other limb.​SRB 1 · p.241
Note the over-2% resultIt is the only test here that distinguishes lymphoedema from venous oedema positively, by showing too fast a clearance rather than too slow. That is a sophisticated point and it is worth making.
And one newer method SRB names
"Lymphofluoroscopy using indocyanine green is excellent method."​SRB 1 · p.246
How much investigation does a swollen limb need: lymphangiography, lymphoscintigraphy, or none at all? Three different positions. S Das 8 p.116 describes lymphangiography at length; SRB 1 p.241 calls lymphoscintigraphy the test of choice; B&L 6 p.73 says investigation in the established case is superfluous
S Das
Gives lymphangiography the full technique and a table of appearances, and introduces it as "of immense value in finding out the causes of lymphoedema, lymph node enlargement and sites of lymph node metastasis".​Das 8 · p.116 Isotope lymphoscintigraphy is not described; the nearest thing is scanning with gallium 67.​Das 8 · p.116
SRB
Keeps lymphangiography, but lists four disadvantages and then displaces it: isotope lymphoscintigraphy "is the test of choice. It is simple and safe", with 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity and the ability to show the thoracic duct and liver.​SRB 1 · p.241 SRB also lists Doppler, abdominal ultrasound, CT, MRI and indocyanine green lymphofluoroscopy.​SRB 1 · p.246
Bailey & Love 28e
Neither test appears. What appears instead is a judgement: "the condition of filariasis is clinically very obvious, and thus investigations in the full-blown case are superfluous." The only tests it names are the nocturnal peripheral blood smear and looking for the parasite in chylous urine, ascites or hydrocele fluid.​B&L 6 · p.73
They are answering different questions, and that is the reconciliation
B&L is writing about established filarial elephantiasis in an endemic area, where the diagnosis is visible from the door and no imaging will change the management, which is conservative. S Das and SRB are writing about a swollen limb of unknown cause, where the imaging is not confirming lymphoedema but finding the obstruction, which may be a pelvic tumour. Both are right about their own patient.
How to answer: let the clinical picture decide, and say so. "In an obvious filarial elephantiasis in an endemic area, the diagnosis is clinical and imaging adds nothing: I would do a nocturnal peripheral smear for microfilariae and look for eosinophilia. In an unexplained unilateral swollen limb, particularly one of rapid onset involving the thigh, I would investigate to find the cause: venous Doppler to exclude deep venous disease, ultrasound or CT of the abdomen and pelvis for a mass obstructing the aortoiliac nodes, and isotope lymphoscintigraphy to confirm lymphatic failure, which is the test of choice because it is simpler and safer than lymphangiography and has about 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity." Mention lymphangiography as the older test and know its two famous appearances, the soap bubble of Hodgkin's and the filling defect of metastasis, but do not offer it as your first choice.

7Differential diagnosis

Cause of a swollen limbWhat separates it from lymphoedema
LymphoedemaStemmer's sign positive; toes and dorsum of foot involved, perimalleolar waist lost; non-pitting once established; does not resolve on overnight elevation​SRB 1 · p.244
Cardiac, renal or hepatic oedemaBilateral, pitting, resolves on elevation, spares the toes, and there are systemic findings. SRB lists cardiac causes, hypoproteinaemia, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome and liver failure​SRB 1 · p.245
Venous disease: deep vein thrombosis, chronic venous insufficiency Dilated veins, pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis in the gaiter area, ulcer above the medial malleolus; toes and dorsum spared. Venous Doppler settles it. Remember both are also listed causes of secondary lymphoedema​SRB 1 · pp.242, 245
LipoedemaSRB's distinguishing list, which is the best answer here: "occurs exclusively in females; begins in puberty; bilateral and symmetrical; trunk may be involved; feet are not involved; not pitting; not related to elevation or compression; MRI shows only fat without fluid"​SRB 1 · p.246
MyxoedemaNon-pitting, but with the systemic features of hypothyroidism​SRB 1 · p.245
Arterial disease and arteriovenous malformationPulses, bruit, warmth, and limb overgrowth in a long-standing malformation​SRB 1 · p.246
Drug-inducedSteroids, oestrogens, nifedipine​SRB 1 · p.246. Ask the question; it saves a workup
Gigantism, and external venous compression by an abdominal tumour Whole-limb overgrowth including bone in the first; in the second, dilated collateral veins and a palpable mass​SRB 1 · p.246
The single most useful discriminator in this table Look at the toes and the dorsum of the foot. Lymphoedema involves them, squares the toes and builds a buffalo hump; venous oedema and lipoedema spare them. Then do Stemmer's sign. Two findings, five seconds, and most of this table is excluded.

8Complications

Infective, and commonest
"Recurrent cellulitis, non-healing ulcers, septicaemia"; "skin thickening, abscess and maggot's formation"; and recurrent streptococcal infection.​SRB 1 · p.246 B&L: "secondary streptococcal infection is common."​B&L 6 · p.72
Lymphangiosarcoma, the Stewart-Treves syndrome
SRB gives the figures and the picture: "lymphangiosarcoma, Stewart-Treves syndrome (0.5%, occurs after 10 years), which presents as multiple bluish satellite nodules in the skin of the limb often with ulceration and haemorrhage. Skin or nodule biopsy is confirmative. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, later even though radical amputation is the treatment, it carries very poor prognosis. This syndrome is usually seen in upper limb after mastectomy."​SRB 1 · p.246 B&L's only reference to it is in the skin chapter: the lymphangiosarcoma variant of angiosarcoma "arises from lymphatic endothelium and can develop in lymphoedematous tissue, particularly an extremity. Proliferation is rapid with early systemic spread."​B&L 45 · p.661
Why this earns a markBecause it answers "why does a post-mastectomy lymphoedema need following up?" A new bluish nodule in a chronically lymphoedematous arm is a lymphangiosarcoma until biopsy says otherwise, and the prognosis is poor. B&L's breast chapter adds chronic lymphoedema to its own list of factors associated with sarcoma.​B&L 58 · p.942
Functional and systemic
Immobility, muscle wasting, severe psychological and social morbidity;​SRB 1 · p.244 and the chylous complications: protein-losing diarrhoea, chylous ascites, chylothorax, chyluria and lymphorrhoea.​SRB 1 · p.244 B&L notes filarial elephantiasis as a leading cause of long-term disability worldwide.​B&L 6 · p.72

9Treatment

Say this first, whatever is asked
The treatment of lymphoedema is conservative, lifelong, and mostly skin care and compression. Every one of the three books agrees on that; where they part company is whether there is any place for an operation at the end of it. Opening with the conservative programme, in order, is what a complete answer looks like.
Physical treatment: the four components
Elevation, exercise and weight reduction. SRB specifies the kind of exercise and the reason: "static isometric activities like prolonged standing or carrying weights should be avoided; rhythmic isotonic movements like swimming or massaging should be encouraged."​SRB 1 · p.246 Rhythmic muscle contraction pumps lymph; static loading does not.
Compression. Multilayered lymphoedema bandaging (MLLB), non-elastic type preferred; graded stockings; and intermittent pneumatic compression devices at pressures over 50 mmHg. It "reduces the oedema, skin changes, lymphorrhoea; softens and supports the inelastic skin; may restore the shape of the limb."​SRB 1 · p.246
And the safety check before you bandage anything"ABPI should be assessed prior using the MLLB."​SRB 1 · p.246 Compressing a limb with arterial disease causes ischaemia. Saying this unprompted is one of the most reliable marks in the case.
Complex decongestive therapy, which is the formal name for the whole programme: "a comprehensive two phase program of elevation, exercise, massaging, and compression wraps. First phase is intensive therapy and second phase is maintenance therapy." Low-stretch wraps in the intensive phase, worn initially for 24 hours; graduated elastic garments in maintenance, giving "maximum pressure of 50 mmHg at the distal part with gradual reduction of pressure in proximal portion".​SRB 1 · p.246
Manual lymphatic drainage, and the order is not arbitrary: "a specialised technique to stimulate the contractility of lymph collecting vessels... done first on the opposite normal side; then trunk, same side trunk; same side proximal; same side distal and later same side distal to proximal fashion, so as to redirect the lymph towards functioning lymphatic territories."​SRB 1 · p.246 You clear the receiving territory before you push lymph into it.
B&L's position on thisIt endorses only one of these and endorses it twice: "in the early stages of limb swelling, intermittent pneumatic compression helps, but the treatment has to be repeated over a prolonged period", and in its summary box, "intermittent pneumatic compression gives some relief."​B&L 6 · p.73 Some relief, repeated indefinitely, is the honest framing.
Skin care, which is not an afterthought
SRB's list, and each item has a target: keratolytics like 5% salicylic acid for the hyperkeratosis; bland emollient, soft or liquid paraffin for the cracking; avoidance of skin sensitisers like some soaps; topical steroids and control of allergy for the eczema; fluconazole and 3% benzoic acid ointment to prevent athlete's foot for the fungal portal of entry; and control of lymphorrhoea and prevention of skin infections.​SRB 1 · p.246 Also "regular washing and keeping the limb clean is very important".​SRB 1 · p.246
The reason to say all thisEvery attack of cellulitis destroys more lymphatics, so preventing the next attack is the only intervention that changes the trajectory of the disease. Skin care is the treatment.
Drugs
Antibiotics: flucloxacillin, erythromycin, long-acting penicillins.​SRB 1 · p.246
Antifungals: topical 1% clotrimazole and systemic griseofulvin 250 to 1000 mg.​SRB 1 · p.246
Diethylcarbamazine citrate 100 mg three times a day for 3 weeks.​SRB 1 · p.246 See the amber box: B&L qualifies when this works.
Benzopyrones: "coumarin (1,2 benzopyrones) derivatives with no anticoagulant effect but increase the lymphatic peristalsis and pumping mechanism along with proteolysis."​SRB 1 · p.246
Two drugs to say you would not useDiuretics: "to reduce the oedema is controversial. It more often causes electrolyte imbalance than being beneficial."​SRB 1 · p.246 The fluid is in the interstitium with its protein; a diuretic cannot move it and only dehydrates the patient.
NSAIDs: "NSAIDs are better avoided in lymphoedema as it may precipitate necrotizing fasciitis."​SRB 1 · p.246 Naming that reason is memorable and it is SRB's own.
Surgery: the three families, and what each is trying to do
Learn the principle of each family rather than the list of eponyms, because the principle is the question.​SRB 1 · pp.246, 247
1. Excisional: take the diseased tissue away. Charles' operation, where "after excising lymphoedematous tissue, area is covered with skin graft". Homans' operation, where the lymphoedematous tissue is excised under raised skin flaps which are then "trimmed to required size and sutured primarily", with "medial and lateral sides of the limb done at separate sittings with 6 months interval".​SRB 1 · pp.246, 247
2. Physiological: build a new route for the lymph. Omentoplasty, because "as omentum contains plenty of lymphatics, omental transfer with pedicle will facilitate lymph drainage". Nodovenous shunt (Nielubowicz), anastomosing an inguinal node to the long saphenous vein. Lymphovenous shunt (O'Brien's), where "at least 4 lymphatics should be anastomosed using 7 zero or 11 zero prolene, using operative microscope". Ileal mucosal patch (Kinmonth), where denuded ileal mucosa on a pedicle is buried in the thigh to communicate with the lymphatics. Also Baumeister lymphatic grafting and autotransplantation of a free lymphatic flap from the opposite side (Trevidic and Cormier) for post-mastectomy lymphoedema.​SRB 1 · pp.246, 247
3. Combined: excise and connect. Sistrunk's operation: "along with excision of lymphoedematous tissue, window cuts in deep fascia is done, so as to allow communication into normal deep lymphatics." Thompson's Swiss-roll operation: "lymphoedematous tissue is excised under the skin flaps. Epidermis and part of the dermis of one of the skin flaps is shaved off using Humby's knife. It is buried under opposite flap, deep to" the deep fascia, so the shaved dermis carries its lymphatics down to the muscle and makes a connection with the deep system.​SRB 1 · pp.246, 247
And one of historical interest only, which SRB labels as such Handley's (1908) buried silk or nylon threads or perforated polyethylene tubes from ankle to mid-abdomen, left for a year: "procedure is only of historical interest."​SRB 1 · p.247 Also Gillies' skin bridge across the thigh and abdomen.​SRB 1 · p.247
Before you offer any of theseRead the amber box below. B&L's position on all of it is that it does not work.
And the one operation all three books endorse
For the scrotum. B&L: "a hydrocele is treated by the usual operation of excision and eversion of the sac with, if necessary, excision of redundant scrotal skin."​B&L 6 · p.73 SRB illustrates scrotal reduction for "extensive scrotal lymphoedema of filarial origin" and reduction with reconstruction for a lymphoedematous penis, "otherwise it may cause urinary problem and sexual dysfunction".​SRB 1 · p.245
Why the genitalia are the exceptionBecause here the swelling causes a functional problem, obstructed micturition and sexual dysfunction, that excision reliably fixes, and the skin cover is redundant and easy to tailor. In a limb the swelling is cosmetic and functional but the operations are disfiguring and the lymphatics are already destroyed. Genital lymphoedema is the clearest surgical indication in this disease, and saying so shows you understand what the surgery is for.
Is there any surgery worth doing for a lymphoedematous limb? A live and total disagreement, and the largest in this case. SRB 1 pp.246, 247 gives two pages of named operations; B&L 6 p.73 says they are hardly ever done because they so rarely work
SRB
Classifies the operations into excisional, physiological and combined, and names more than a dozen: Charles', Homans', omentoplasty, nodovenous shunt (Nielubowicz), lymphovenous shunt (O'Brien's), ileal mucosal patch (Kinmonth), Sistrunk's, Thompson's Swiss roll, Baumeister lymphatic grafting, free lymphatic flap autotransplantation (Trevidic and Cormier), Gillies' skin bridge, with Handley's threads marked as historical. It gives operative detail down to suture size: "at least 4 lymphatics should be anastomosed using 7 zero or 11 zero prolene, using operative microscope."​SRB 1 · pp.246, 247 No operation is described as ineffective.
Bailey & Love 28e
Two sentences, both dismissive, and it is the only thing it says about limb surgery. "Operations for reducing the size of the limb are hardly ever done these days because the procedures are so rarely successful."​B&L 6 · p.73 And in its summary box: "the value of various surgical procedures is largely unproven and hence they are rarely performed."​B&L 6 · p.73 Not one of SRB's eponyms appears anywhere in the chapter. What B&L does endorse is medical treatment, intermittent pneumatic compression, and operation on the scrotum for a hydrocele with excision of redundant skin.​B&L 6 · p.73
Why they differ, which is the part worth understanding
Both are right about different things. The surgery has two honest problems. Excisional operations work but at a price: Charles' operation does reduce a huge limb, and leaves a grafted, cosmetically poor, often chronically ulcerated leg. Physiological operations are elegant but the premise is weak: by the time a limb is bad enough to operate on, the superficial lymphatics are fibrosed and there is nothing patent left to anastomose, which is why the shunts and grafts have never produced durable published results. B&L is making an evidence judgement. SRB is a surgical manual for an examination in which these operations are asked about by name, and it reports them without endorsing their outcomes. Note that SRB does not actually claim they work either; it describes them.
How to answer: this is a question about priorities, so answer it as one. Lead with the conservative programme, then name the operations, then give B&L's verdict yourself before the examiner does.

"The treatment of lymphoedema is overwhelmingly conservative and lifelong: elevation, rhythmic isotonic exercise, weight reduction, meticulous skin and nail care with treatment of interdigital fungal infection, prompt antibiotics for every attack of cellulitis, and sustained compression by multilayer bandaging and graded stockings, with the ankle-brachial pressure index checked before any compression is applied. Diethylcarbamazine if it is filarial. Diuretics are not useful and NSAIDs are avoided because they may precipitate necrotising fasciitis.

Surgery is reserved for the minority. It falls into three groups: excisional, such as Charles' operation with skin grafting and Homans' operation under skin flaps; physiological, which attempt to create a route from the diseased superficial to the normal deep lymphatics, such as omentoplasty, nodovenous and lymphovenous shunts and the ileal mucosal patch; and combined, such as Sistrunk's windows in the deep fascia and Thompson's buried dermal flap. I would add that Bailey and Love 28e regards these limb-reduction operations as rarely performed and of largely unproven value, because once the limb is bad enough to operate on the superficial lymphatics are already fibrosed. The clearest surgical indication is genital lymphoedema, where scrotal or penile reduction relieves a functional problem."

For an Indian written paper, write SRB's three-group classification with the eponyms, because the marks are there, and add B&L's judgement as a closing sentence. That gets both marks and credibility.
Diethylcarbamazine: does it help once elephantiasis is established? A live disagreement about timing. SRB 1 p.246 lists DEC as treatment without qualification; B&L 6 p.73 restricts it to the early stage
SRB
Lists it among the conservative measures with a dose and no stage qualifier: "diethyl carbamazine citrate (DEC) 100 mg TID for 3 weeks."​SRB 1 · p.246 It sits in the same list as antibiotics, antifungals, compression and skin care, as part of the standard programme.
Bailey & Love 28e
Puts a clear boundary on it: "medical treatment with diethylcarbamazine is very effective in the early stages before the gross deformities of elephantiasis have developed."​B&L 6 · p.73 Its summary box says the same in fewer words: "early cases are very amenable to medical treatment."​B&L 6 · p.73 The implication is that in established elephantiasis DEC is not the answer.
Why both are defensible
DEC kills the parasite. It cannot undo fibrosis. In early disease, where the swelling is still fluid and the lymphatics still patent, killing the worms arrests and may reverse the process, which is B&L's point. In established elephantiasis the limb will not improve, but there is still a reason to give it: the patient is infective to mosquitoes, and treating the carrier is a public health measure as much as a personal one. SRB's placement of DEC in the standard list is not wrong, it is just not a claim that the limb will shrink.
How to answer: give the drug with its indication and the limit of what it does. "I would give diethylcarbamazine citrate, 100 mg three times daily for three weeks, if the lymphoedema is filarial. It is very effective in the early stages, before the gross deformity of elephantiasis has developed, because it kills the parasite and the lymphatics are still patent. In established elephantiasis it will not reduce the limb, because the swelling is fibrosis rather than fluid, but it is still given to clear the microfilaraemia, since the patient is a reservoir for transmission." That last clause is the part most candidates miss, and it is the difference between treating a limb and treating a disease.

10Rapid-fire viva

Define lymphoedema.

Accumulation of protein-rich lymph in the extracellular, extravascular compartment, commonly the subcutaneous tissue, due to defective lymphatic drainage.​SRB 1 · p.241 The words that matter are protein rich, because the protein drives the fibrosis that makes the oedema non-pitting.

One sign that separates lymphoedema from every other swollen limb.

Stemmer's sign: the skin over the dorsum of the foot cannot be pinched, because of subcutaneous fibrosis.​SRB 1 · p.244 It tests fibrosis, not fluid, which is why it is negative in cardiac, renal, hepatic and venous oedema.

Classify lymphoedema.

Kinmonth: primary, with no identifiable lymphatic disease, and secondary, acquired from a definite cause, which is the commoner form. Primary is subdivided by age of onset: congenita at birth to two years (10%, familial form Nonne-Milroy's disease, autosomal dominant); praecox at puberty up to about 35 (80%, familial form Letessier-Meige's); and tarda after 35.​SRB 1 · p.242

What is Browse's classification, and why is it more useful?

A lymphangiographic classification: congenital hyperplasia 10%, distal obliteration 80%, proximal obliteration 10%.​SRB 1 · p.241 It is more useful because it maps onto the bedside picture and onto management. Distal disease is bilateral, slowly progressive, starts at the ankle, affects young women. Proximal disease is unilateral, rapidly progressive, involves the thigh and is caused by an aortoiliac nodal block, so that is the patient in whom you must look for a pelvic malignancy.

Causes of secondary lymphoedema.

Surgery, particularly axillary clearance or inguinal block dissection; radiotherapy to the same nodal basin; filariasis; advanced malignancy with hard fixed nodes; infection including tuberculosis, syphilis and fungal; trauma; and rarely rheumatoid arthritis, insect and snake bites, deep vein thrombosis and chronic venous insufficiency.​SRB 1 · p.242 Secondary lymphoedema develops rapidly, which is a useful historical pointer.

Why does lymphoedema not involve the muscles?

Because the disease is confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue, outside the deep fascia. Only the superficial lymphatics are involved; the deep lymphatics are normal, and unlike the superficial and deep veins the two lymphatic systems do not communicate with each other.​SRB 1 · pp.242, 244 The muscles are normal and may even hypertrophy.

What is the principle behind the physiological operations?

To create a communication between the diseased superficial lymphatics and the normal deep ones, which do not naturally communicate. That is what Sistrunk's windows in the deep fascia, Thompson's buried shaved dermal flap, the nodovenous and lymphovenous shunts, the ileal mucosal patch and omentoplasty are all attempting to do.​SRB 1 · pp.244, 246, 247

Grade this lymphoedema.

Latent, subclinical with no apparent swelling. Grade I, pitting oedema that more or less disappears on elevation. Grade II, non-pitting oedema that does not reduce on elevation. Grade III, oedema with irreversible skin changes, fibrosis, papillae and fissuring.​SRB 1 · p.245 There is also a volumetric scale: mild under 20% excess limb volume, moderate 20 to 40%, severe over 40%.

Which investigation is the test of choice, and what does it show?

Isotope lymphoscintigraphy. Technetium-labelled sulphide colloid or radioiodinated albumin is injected into a web space and taken up specifically by lymphatics; inguinal node activity is measured at 30 and 60 minutes. Normal uptake is 0.6 to 1.6%; under 0.3% at 30 minutes is diagnostic of lymphoedema, and over 2% suggests venous oedema with rapid clearance. Sensitivity about 90%, specificity 100%.​SRB 1 · p.241

How do you distinguish lymphoedema from lipoedema?

Lipoedema occurs exclusively in women, begins at puberty, is bilateral and symmetrical, may involve the trunk, and crucially spares the feet. It is non-pitting but unrelated to elevation or compression, and MRI shows fat without fluid.​SRB 1 · p.246 Lymphoedema involves the foot and the toes and has a positive Stemmer's sign.

Why do you not give diuretics?

Because the fluid is protein-rich interstitial fluid outside the vascular compartment; a diuretic cannot mobilise it and more often causes electrolyte imbalance than benefit.​SRB 1 · p.246

Any drug you would specifically avoid?

NSAIDs, because SRB notes they may precipitate necrotising fasciitis in a lymphoedematous limb.​SRB 1 · p.246 Pain is relieved by other means.

What would you check before applying compression bandaging?

The ankle-brachial pressure index.​SRB 1 · p.246 Compressing a limb with significant arterial disease causes ischaemia.

A patient with a post-mastectomy lymphoedematous arm develops bluish nodules in the skin. What is it?

Lymphangiosarcoma, the Stewart-Treves syndrome: multiple bluish satellite nodules, often ulcerating and bleeding, occurring in about 0.5% and typically after ten years, most often in the upper limb after mastectomy. Skin or nodule biopsy confirms it. Prognosis is very poor even with radical amputation.​SRB 1 · p.246 Bailey and Love describes the same tumour as the lymphangiosarcoma variant of angiosarcoma, arising from lymphatic endothelium in lymphoedematous tissue with rapid proliferation and early systemic spread.​B&L 45 · p.661

Which parasite causes filarial lymphoedema, and which mosquito?

Wuchereria bancrofti, with Brugia malayi and Brugia timori responsible in about 10%.​B&L 6 · p.72 In India the vector is Culex fatigans; man is the definitive host, the female mosquito the intermediate host, and no animal reservoir is known.​SRB 1 · p.242

When would you take the blood smear for microfilariae, and why?

At night, classically between 10 pm and 4 am, because the microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity matched to the night-biting habit of Culex and the sleeping habit of the host.​SRB 1 · p.242​Das 8 · p.115 Eosinophilia is also common, and the parasite may be found in chylous urine, ascites or hydrocele fluid.​B&L 6 · p.73

Why does filarial disease take years to become severe if the worms do not multiply in the host?

Because they do not multiply: one microfilaria produces one infective larva, and the microfilaria never multiplies in mosquito or human. Severity comes from repeated infective bites over years, and from the fibrosis left by recurrent attacks of lymphangitis, not from an expanding parasite load.​SRB 1 · p.243​B&L 6 · p.72

How do you treat established filarial elephantiasis of the leg?

Conservatively and for life: elevation, rhythmic isotonic exercise, weight reduction, meticulous skin and interdigital care with antifungals, prompt antibiotics for every cellulitis, and sustained compression by multilayer bandaging and graded stockings, with the ABPI checked first. Diethylcarbamazine to clear microfilaraemia, though it will not reduce an established limb.​SRB 1 · p.246​B&L 6 · p.73 Bailey and Love regards limb-reduction operations as rarely performed and of largely unproven value.​B&L 6 · p.73

Name the operations for lymphoedema, grouped.

Excisional: Charles' operation, excision with skin grafting; Homans' operation, excision under skin flaps. Physiological: omentoplasty; nodovenous shunt (Nielubowicz); lymphovenous shunt (O'Brien's); ileal mucosal patch (Kinmonth); Baumeister lymphatic grafting; free lymphatic flap autotransplantation. Combined: Sistrunk's operation, excision plus windows in the deep fascia; Thompson's Swiss-roll operation, excision plus a shaved dermal flap buried against the muscle.​SRB 1 · pp.246, 247 Handley's buried threads are of historical interest only.

Which lymphoedema has the clearest indication for surgery?

Genital. Scrotal and penile lymphoedema cause urinary and sexual dysfunction that reduction surgery reliably relieves, and both books endorse operating there: Bailey and Love for excision and eversion of the hydrocele sac with excision of redundant scrotal skin,​B&L 6 · p.73 SRB for scrotal reduction and for penile reduction with reconstruction.​SRB 1 · p.245 Breast lymphoedema may need reduction mammoplasty.

What is podoconiosis?

Endemic, non-filarial elephantiasis, common in Africa and seen in barefoot workers, caused by destruction of lymphatics by silica from soil containing alkaline volcanic rock.​SRB 1 · p.244

In what order would you perform manual lymphatic drainage, and why?

Opposite normal side first, then the trunk, then the trunk on the affected side, then the affected limb proximally, then distally, and finally distal to proximal, so as to redirect lymph towards functioning lymphatic territories.​SRB 1 · p.246 You clear the receiving territory before pushing lymph into it.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. Bailey & Love 28e has no lymphatic system chapter. Lymphoedema appears in exactly three places, and the pearl at the top of this case lists all three: the substantive discussion is in ch.6, "Tropical infections and infestations", pp.72 and 73, under filariasis, and it covers filarial lymphoedema only; there is one sentence in ch.45 p.661 on lymphangiosarcoma arising in lymphoedematous tissue; and ch.58 treats it as a complication of axillary surgery and irradiation. So the classification, the grading, the investigations and every named operation in this case come from SRB ch.1 pp.241 to 247, with the clinical examination from S Das ch.8, whose chapter contains no operations for lymphoedema and none of the eponyms. Two amber boxes set out the real disagreements: whether limb surgery is worth doing at all, and whether diethylcarbamazine helps once elephantiasis is established. A third covers how much investigation an obviously filarial limb needs.
